important_taxonomic_note: Downy mildew is a disease complex with several possible oomycete pathogens globally. The Egypt-specific maize studies reviewed here identify P. sorghi as the causal pathogen.

documented_locations: Sakha Experimental Station, Kafr El-Sheikh Governorate
Gemmeiza Agricultural Research Station, Gharbia Governorate
egypt_distribution.field_pattern: The 2001 Egyptian study reported that the disease was not common nationally at that time but produced a sudden serious outbreak in the Nile Delta in 1989, especially in maize near forage sorghum. It was also detected at Gemmeiza.
egypt_distribution.recent_evidence_limit: The sources reviewed do not establish current nationwide incidence or a current governorate-level prevalence map.

early_stage: Pale green to yellow chlorotic streaks on young leaves
Chlorotic mottling or narrow longitudinal stripes
Symptoms may appear first on leaves of young seedlings
characteristic_leaf_symptoms: White, grey-white, or downy growth on the lower leaf surface, especially during humid nights or mornings
Long chlorotic stripes running parallel to leaf veins
Yellow stripes may widen, merge, and form blotches
Leaves become narrow, erect, pale, and sometimes shredded
whole_plant_symptoms: Excessive tillering or bushy plant appearance
Malformed tassels with leafy proliferation or 'crazy top' symptoms
Malformed ears, poor ear emergence, or ears with few/no developed kernels
Premature death when infection occurs at the seedling stage
advanced_symptoms: Chlorotic leaves turn yellow-brown, reddish-brown, or necrotic
Leaves may dry, shred, or die prematurely
Plants may remain sterile or produce small, poorly filled ears
image_annotation_targets: white downy growth on the lower leaf surface
leaf width and erectness compared with healthy plants
leaf shredding and necrotic stripe coalescence
small or sterile ears and poor grain formation

symptoms: white-grey downy growth on leaf undersides
distribution_on_plant: Often most visible on young and newly emerging leaves; systemic infection can affect the whole plant, including leaves, tassels, ears, and growing points.
progression: Seedling or young plants develop chlorosis, mottling, or narrow yellow stripes.
White-grey downy sporulation appears on leaf undersides under humid conditions.
Stripes widen and coalesce; leaves become narrow, erect, pale, and may shred.
Systemically infected plants become stunted and may tiller excessively.
Tassels and ears can become malformed, with poor grain production or complete sterility.
Early severe infection may kill seedlings or entire plants before flowering.

environment.humidity: High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness favour sporulation and infection.
environment.temperature: Warm, humid conditions favour disease development; an Egypt-specific temperature threshold was not identified in the reviewed field studies.
environment.leaf_wetness: Night dew, rain, irrigation, and humid periods encourage downy growth and airborne sporangial spread.
inoculum_sources: nearby forage sorghum and Sudan grass acting as inoculum sources
environment.egypt_context: Egyptian studies identified outbreaks near forage sorghum in the Nile Delta and used Sudan grass infector rows at Gemmeiza to produce inoculum.

seed_transmission_evidence_in_egypt.finding: An Egyptian study tested 31 maize seed samples and detected P. sorghi infection in seed tissues at levels ranging from 0.2% to 24%.
seed_transmission_evidence_in_egypt.field_relationship: Approximately 60% of infected seed inoculum was estimated to be transmitted to developing maize plants in the field trials.

similar_diseases.name: Brown Stripe Downy Mildew
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Produces narrow yellow-to-brown stripes but generally lacks the systemic malformation and leafy tassel/ear symptoms typical of sorghum downy mildew.

similar_diseases.name: Maize Dwarf Mosaic
similar_diseases.visual_difference: May cause chlorotic striping and stunting, but does not produce the characteristic white downy growth on leaf undersides.

similar_diseases.name: Nutrient deficiency or herbicide injury
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Can cause yellow striping or chlorosis but normally lacks visible downy sporulation and systemic reproductive malformation.

diagnostic_caution: White downy growth is highly useful visually but may be temporary and absent in dry conditions. Confirm suspected cases by microscopy, molecular testing, or laboratory identification of Peronosclerospora sorghi. Do not confuse downy mildew with viral chlorotic striping or nutrient/herbicide injury.
